progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: C13 (the salt at equivalence takes after its stronger parent; ethanoate makes the equivalence point basic, ammonium acidic; the 8.72 equivalence pH; the steep jump; the ethanoic acid curve's shape near equivalence). C12 (titration, titre, equivalence point; the titre counts moles of acid, weak or strong; n = cV). C11 (a weak acid with its conjugate base is a buffer; equal amounts give pH = pKa). C10 (pKa = −log Ka, Ka = 10⁻ᵖᴷᵃ). C08 (a weak acid stays mostly un-ionised; its pH is higher than a strong acid's at the same concentration). C07 (pH of a strong acid, [H₃O⁺] = c). C05 (strong and weak). Year 11 (solutions of ions conduct electricity because the ions move). Not assumed: titration curve, buffer region as a curve feature, half-equivalence point, conductivity graph, how fast different ions carry charge.
progression.startsWith: Read axes and starting pH on a reaction profile. The video opens: Two beakers, each with twenty five point zero zero millilitres of acid at zero point one zero zero moles per litre. One is hydrochloric acid, one is ethanoic acid. Add the same sodium hydroxide to each, measure the pH after every portion, and plot it.
progression.stopsAfter: reading a titration curve's axes and starting pH and inferring strength at equal concentration; identifying the buffer region of a weak acid curve and explaining it; finding the equivalence point in the middle of the steep jump and using its volume to calculate a concentration; reading pKa at half the equivalence volume and calculating Ka; explaining the equivalence pH and the shorter jump of a weak acid; recognising the strong acid/weak base profile; explaining the conductivity graphs of a strong and a weak acid titrated with sodium hydroxide, and finding equivalence from each. No indicator choice (chem-m6-c13), no pH calculations at every region (site Extension), no weak/weak curves, no conductometric method or line-intersection reading (chem-m6-c15), no back titration (chem-m6-c15).
progression.nextLesson: when a direct titration won't work: back titrations and conductivity titrations (route chem-m6-c15).

teaching.task: Hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid at the same concentration, titrated with the same base, give two very different pH curves and two different conductivity graphs. What can those profiles tell you about an acid: strong or weak, where equivalence is, how much acid there is, and even its Ka?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the same acid concentration and the same base give two different curves; each feature carries information (1); (2) a curve plots the flask's pH against the volume of titrant; at the start, the strong acid is fully ionised (pH 1.000) and the weak acid mostly whole (2.87): at equal concentration, a higher start means a weaker acid (2); (3) early on, the strong acid's pH stays low because plenty of hydronium is left; the weak acid's climbs, then levels, because base turns it into a buffer of weak acid and conjugate base: the buffer region (3); (4) at half the equivalence volume the partners are equal, so pH = pKa: 4.74, and Ka = 10⁻⁴·⁷⁴ (4); (5) the equivalence point is in the middle of the steepest part; both acids need 25.00 mL, because a titre counts moles, not strength; that volume gives the concentration (5); (6) the equivalence pH follows the salt (7.00 against 8.72); the weak acid's jump is shorter because its buffer held the pH up until the last drops (6); (7) a strong acid with a weak base: an acidic equivalence point and a low jump, then a level stretch near 9 because excess ammonia and ammonium form a buffer (7); (8) conductivity: hydronium and hydroxide conduct best; in HCl, fast hydronium is replaced by slower sodium, so conductivity falls to a minimum at equivalence, then rises with excess hydroxide (8); (9) ethanoic acid starts with few ions, so conductivity starts low, rises gently as sodium and ethanoate form, then steeply after equivalence: equivalence at the bend (9); memory aid (10); two attempts and brief feedback (11 to 14); decision rule and handoff (15); key notes (16).
teaching.conversationalApproach: one contrast carries the video: hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid at the same concentration, titrated with the same base, give two very different pH curves and two different conductivity graphs. Each feature is read for its cause in turn: the starting pH (fully ionised against mostly whole), the buffer region (base turns the weak acid into a buffer), half-equivalence (equal partners, so pH = pKa and Ka follows), the equivalence point in the middle of the jump (the same 25.00 mL, because a titre counts moles), the equivalence pH and jump length, a strong acid with a weak base, and conductivity (fast hydronium replaced by slower sodium gives a V; a weak acid gives a bend). Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Two beakers, each with twenty five point zero zero millilitres of acid at zero point one zero zero moles per litre. One is hydrochloric acid, one is ethanoic acid. Add the same sodium hydroxide to each, measure the pH after every portion, and plot it. You get two very different curves. Every bend in them carries information: whether the acid is strong or weak, how much there is, even its K a. So how do you read one?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A student titrated 20.00 mL of an acid, HA, with 0.1000 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution and plotted the titration curve shown. (a) Using two features of the curve, identify whether HA is a strong or a weak acid. (b) Calculate the concentration of HA. (c) Determine the Ka of HA." The coded curve (author note h) has grid lines every 5 mL and every pH unit, and labelled dots at 0.0 mL (pH 2.79), 5.0 mL (4.10), 10.0 mL (4.57), 15.0 mL (5.05), 20.0 mL (8.63, in the middle of the jump) and 25.0 mL (12.05). New acid and new volumes; the student must find the equivalence volume in the jump, halve it and read the pH. Crossed mistake: "pKa = 8.63, the pH at equivalence" (site L17 Activity A item 2). (A2) "0.100 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution is added to 20.00 mL of hydrochloric acid, and the conductivity is measured. The conductivity falls to a minimum when 16.0 mL of sodium hydroxide has been added, then rises. (a) Explain the shape of the conductivity graph. (b) Calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid." The graph is shown (author note k). Tests the conductivity trend and the equivalence volume from a graph. Crossed mistake: "it falls because the ions are used up" (site L18 card 3's Common Error, inverted: the number of ions stays about the same before equivalence).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate titration curves and conductivity graphs to analyse data to indicate characteristic reaction profiles, for example:; strong acid/strong base; strong acid/weak base; weak acid/strong base (ACSCH080, ACSCH102)" this video starts from the route's axes and starting pH on a reaction profile and stops at inferring strengths, the equivalence region and a conductivity trend. It teaches: what a titration curve plots (pH in the flask against volume of titrant added); the starting pH as evidence of strength at equal concentration (C05 and C08 callbacks); the early part of each curve, with the weak acid's buffer region (C11 callback: each portion of base makes a weak acid and conjugate base mixture); the half-equivalence point, where pH = pKa, and Ka from it (C10 and C11 callbacks); the equivalence point in the middle of the steepest part, the same volume for a strong and a weak acid at equal moles (C12 callback), and the concentration from that volume; the equivalence pH from the salt (C13 callback, one line) and why the weak acid's jump is shorter; the strong acid/weak base profile (an acidic equivalence point and a high-pH buffer after it); conductivity graphs for hydrochloric and ethanoic acid titrated with sodium hydroxide, explained by which ions are replaced and how well they conduct. Not here: the indicator equilibrium, transition ranges and indicator choice (chem-m6-c13, one callback only); calculating the pH at every region of a curve (site card 5, labelled Extension; the start and equivalence calculations are C08 and C13 callbacks, not repeated); the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation by name or in log form (C11 decision); weak acid with weak base curves (site Extension); polyprotic curves (site worksheet corrections); using a conductivity titration as a method, reading equivalence from the intersection of two straight lines, and coloured or cloudy samples (chem-m6-c15, the next video, with back titration); barium hydroxide with sulfuric acid; error direction for indicator choices (chem-m6-g04).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout: the hydrochloric acid curve pale blue, the ethanoic acid curve teal (C13), the hydrochloric acid with ammonia curve amber; H₃O⁺ teal token, OH⁻ violet, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ small grey spectators, ethanoate grey-violet (C01, C03, C11); the titrant navy (C12); feature markers white rings. Board layout (constant, C03, C11 and C13): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the graph, large; readings write beside the feature they describe and dim when the next is read; a plate sits small at the right only when it carries the explanation. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 21 Oct): `m6-ph-meter-probe-beaker-v1.png` (hook, coded readout ticking as portions are added; beaker labelled in code), `m6-burette-clamp-stand-v1.png` (hook thumbnail, the titrant), `m5x-ammonia-bottle-v1.png` (scene 7, small), `m6-conductivity-meter-titration-v1.png` (inspected: two probes clamped in a stirred beaker on a magnetic stirrer, a handheld meter with a blank screen, no person or hand; scenes 8, 9 and attempt 2, with a coded readout on its blank screen). No new plates needed. No human figures.
design.transitionPlan: The burette and two pH meter plates open the hook as the lineGraph axes draw and both curves trace point by point; feature rings land on the curves one feature per scene while earlier readings dim; the C11 ratio bar fills beside the buffer region and the half-volume caliper folds to drop the pKa line; the magnifier inset opens on both jumps for the equivalence volume and pH; the ammonia curve draws over the dimmed curves; the board clears for the conductivity meter plate, the proton hop along water and the conductivity graph with its ion tally of tokens, the HCl V dimming as the ethanoic bend draws; the memory aid writes large; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the givens on the card and curve; the decision rule card and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
